Senses.Explanation: A winter-melon seal is a crude stamp of certification: it marks people as approved while supplying only the shape of a true seal. Chan masters use the image to attack indiscriminate recognition, formulaic authorization, and premature claims of transmission. Yongjue condemns teachers who stamp one another; Tianyin attacks people determined to stamp students; Tian’an describes seasonal teachers stamping half-ripe practitioners; and Lianfeng caps Huangbo’s threatened blows as the same crude stamp.

Senses.Explanation: ‘The winter melon is bluntly straight; the bottle gourd bends in a curve’ answers difficult questions with the plain difference between two common shapes. Masters use the old pair to interrupt abstract explanation and press what is visible in the situation at hand. Poshan Haiming inserts the vegetables into a playful turn on a scripture and asks where the Buddha can turn. Feiyin Tongrong asks a disciple how the pair applies to the person before him; the disciple replies with his eyebrows, and Feiyin accepts it. Huijue Yi asks how to speak of understanding when the matter resists hearing and visible form, then answers by moving his whisk and naming the two vegetables. Wuzhun Shifan asks what ninety summer days have achieved and gives the pair as his reply. Yuansou Xingduan is asked about the higher matter after a ceremonial blessing. He answers with the winter melon and gourd, then continues the exchange through a different old encounter.

Senses.Explanation: To chew over is to find material for conceptual working, verbal rumination, or sustained investigation. Chan records extend the bodily action to sayings and public cases: Yunxi Langting Ting tells beginners to “chew over a ready-made sentence that cannot be knocked down” and repeats “chew it over, chew it over” (咬嚼來、咬嚼去); the same record says Wujin spent his whole life unable to chew through “the bowl-carrying public case” (托缽公案). Senses.Explanation: Scoop water and the moon is in your hands; touch the flowers and their fragrance fills your sleeves. Direct participation reveals the image without taking possession of the moon or perfume. Current deployments include Guxue Zhenzhe in J28nB208, Shaweng Huihai in J29nB230, Lianyue Daozheng in J29nB236, and Doushuai Zongjian in J33nB285. The full paired image remains the lexical unit. The moon is a reflection in water; no source asks for a literal moon in the hand.

Senses.Explanation: Fresh sun and moon; a world made new announces that the whole occasion has opened anew. Faxi raises a whisk at New Year and calls the sun, moon, and world fresh. Zishui says it at the opening of a new hall. Yezhu uses it on taking up a new temple and immediately speaks of staff and shout in action. Zhitan gives it as an answer about the first bloom of spring. Kaifu says that one who recognizes the older case meets a fresh world. Tanfang opens an installation address with it. Shuzhong gives it while appointing a head monk and says the right person can shoulder the task.

Nanquan cuts the cat in two
Senses.Explanation: Nanquan's public cat-cutting case, not a general instruction to cut a cat. This graph form occurs 156 times in 53 allowlisted texts and names the same event as the alternative cat graph. The east and west halls fight over a cat; Nanquan holds it up and says that an answer will spare it; the assembly gives no answer and he cuts it in two. When Zhaozhou returns, he puts a sandal on his head and leaves; Nanquan says that his presence would have saved the cat. Later records make the phrase a case title, a public question, a verse subject, and a cited precedent. A question explicitly invokes the major precept against killing and asks why Nanquan cut the cat and Guizong cut the snake; Miyun Yuanwu tells the questioner to repent. Dahui Zonggao reports that students call the two cases ‘timely wondrous function’ or ‘great function appearing without retaining rules,’ then rejects both accounts. The entry preserves the hard precept question and Dahui's rejection without inventing a rationale for the killing.
Senses.Note: The two written cat forms are searchable family members but name one event. The full event without the contiguous headword is family evidence; six exact witnesses across six sources clear the floor. Case title, verse, and later question are deployments of the same event, not separate things. The precept-violation dispute is reported without ruling whether the act is justified.

Senses.PreferredTarget: Guizong's snake-cutting case
Senses.Explanation: Guizong's snake-cutting case is the chief Chan referent of the compact phrase ‘cut the snake.’ Guizong Zhichang cut a passing snake with a hoe, an unnamed lecture monk called him coarse, Guizong raised the hoe as ‘coarse,’ made a cutting gesture as ‘fine,’ and asked where that lecturer had seen him cut the snake. Later masters ask about ‘the old man's snake-cutting,’ pair it with Nanquan cutting the cat and Dasui burning the clearing, turn ‘the snake-cutter’ into a stock agent noun, and compare Guizong's act with raising the whisk. The case is also explicitly challenged from the precepts: records ask why Guizong cut the snake when killing living beings is a major precept or when a precept-keeper will not tread on living grass. One answer tells the questioner to repent; another asks, ‘is it cutting, or is it killing?’ A sermon quoting the rule to rescue animals from killing then asks what could have saved Guizong's snake. The corpus does not call this snake poisonous and does not say it threatened the community.
Senses.Note: The exact expression occurs 137 times in 65 allowlisted texts, across core case retellings, public questions, sermons, verse, and commentarial collections. Its plain verbal sense and case-label use name the same act, so item 8 does not require a split. The later record supplies incompatible appraisals rather than different referents: one verse calls the cutting compassion, Dahui rejects familiar functional explanations, and Tianran condemns imitating the case as license for unrestrained conduct. They remain reported evidence within one sense, not a menu of dictionary readings.

Senses.Explanation: Cutting the cat names Nanquan’s canonical action and functions as a later benchmark for decisive conduct. This graph form is attested and is the orthographic counterpart of “cut the cat” (斬猫), not a different event. In the records it abbreviates the public case in which the east and west halls fight over a cat; Nanquan holds it up and says, “If you can speak, I will not cut it,” the assembly gives no answer, and he cuts the cat in two. When Zhaozhou returns, he puts a sandal on his head and leaves; Nanquan says that had he been there, he would have saved the cat. The phrase functions as case narration and title, an object of questions, a subject for verses, and a cited precedent. One public exchange explicitly asks, “Killing living beings is a major precept; why did Nanquan cut the cat and Guizong cut the snake?”; Miyun Yuanwu tells the questioner to repent. Another sermon quotes the rule to rescue animals from killing and asks how Nanquan's cat and Guizong's snake could have been saved. These passages establish the corpus's own precept relation without stating Nanquan's intention. Asked for the case's import, Jueyin answers only, “It takes Nanquan” (須是南泉始得). Dahui reports and rejects students' labels “timely wondrous function” and “great function appears, not retaining rules.”

Senses.Explanation: Cut off the head while seeking life is an impossible rescue: the very act taken to find life removes what must remain alive. Chan masters repeatedly oppose it to adding another head atop one’s own, placing both images on rejected sides of a verbal choice. Poshan applies the pair first to ‘mind/buddha’ wording and again to seeking a decision from oneself or another; Tianyin applies it to saying exertion is absent or present; and Fachang applies it to saying one understands or does not.

Senses.Explanation: Blinking the eyes and lifting the brows: Chan speakers name these tiny facial motions as possible cues, while asking whether the motion actually reaches its listener. Shixi Xinyue sets Mazu's blinking and brow lifting beside Shishuang's gritted teeth and calls such visible moves a temporary side road. Jieweizhou Xingzhou uses the phrase in a verse on what ordinary motions disclose. Juyun Chuiwan Guangzhen lists it with blows, shouts, and other ancestral moves, then tests what those moves accomplish. Yunwai Xingze criticizes teachers who urge imitation of a blink or raised brow without the needed work. Jiqi Hongchu calls the fist, finger, eyes, and brows a ghostly display when taken as the answer. Yikui Yuankui says that even blinking and lifting the brows may conceal great skill under an awkward appearance. Zhufeng Zhenxu invites anyone whose gestures and steps are clear to show discerning sight.
